# DIRseq as a method for predicting drug-interacting residues of intrinsically disordered proteins from sequences

## Authors

- Matt MacAinsh<sup>1</sup>
- Sanbo Qin<sup>1</sup>
- Huan-Xiang Zhou<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-9020-0302](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9020-0302)) †

### Affiliations

1. Department of Chemistry, University of Illinois Chicago Chicago United States ([ROR:02mpq6x41](https://ror.org/02mpq6x41))
2. Department of Physics, University of Illinois Chicago Chicago United States ([ROR:02mpq6x41](https://ror.org/02mpq6x41))

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are now well-recognized as drug targets. Identifying drug-interacting residues is valuable for both optimizing compounds and elucidating the mechanism of action. Currently, NMR chemical shift perturbation and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are the primary tools for this purpose. Here, we present DIRseq, a fast method for predicting drug-interacting residues from the amino-acid sequence. All residues contribute to the propensity of a particular residue to be drug-interacting; the contributing factor of each residue has an amplitude that is determined by its amino-acid type and attenuates with increasing sequence distance from the particular residue. DIRseq predictions match well with drug-interacting residues identified by NMR chemical shift perturbation and other methods, including residues L22WK24 and Q52WFT55 in the tumor suppressor protein p53. These successes augur well for deciphering the sequence code for IDP-drug binding. DIRseq is available as a web server at https://zhougroup-uic.github.io/DIRseq/ and has many applications, such as virtual screening against IDPs and designing IDP fragments for in-depth NMR and MD studies.

## Introduction

Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are now recognized as important drug targets (Joshi and Vendruscolo, 2015; Saurabh et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Uversky, 2024). For structured protein targets, a crucial step in characterizing drug binding is identifying the drug-binding pocket. Although an IDP can be locked into a specific conformation by a drug molecule in rare cases (Peterson et al., 2004), the prevailing scenario is that the protein remains disordered upon drug binding (Woods et al., 2011; Ono et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2013; De Mol et al., 2016; Heller et al., 2020; Iwaya et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Heller et al., 2024). Consequently, the IDP-drug complex typically samples a vast conformational space, and the drug molecule only exhibits preferences, rather than exclusiveness, for interacting with subsets of residues (Jin et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022). Such drug-interacting residues, akin to binding pockets in structured proteins, are key to optimizing compounds (Robustelli et al., 2022; Iconaru et al., 2015; Basu et al., 2023) and elucidating the mechanism of action (Woods et al., 2011; De Mol et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2021; Iconaru et al., 2015; Basu et al., 2023).

NMR chemical shift perturbation (CSP) is the best experimental method for identifying drug-interacting residues and has been applied to many IDPs (Ono et al., 2012; De Mol et al., 2016; Iwaya et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Heller et al., 2024; Iconaru et al., 2015; Basu et al., 2023; Hammoudeh et al., 2009; Lamberto et al., 2009; Krishnan et al., 2014; Tatenhorst et al., 2016; Ahmed et al., 2017; Kocis et al., 2017; Neira et al., 2017; Ruan et al., 2021; Iruela et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022). Aromatic residues are frequently among drug-interacting residues (Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Iconaru et al., 2015; Basu et al., 2023; Lamberto et al., 2009; Tatenhorst et al., 2016; Ruan et al., 2021). This is understandable as drug molecules typically are rich in aromatic rings (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1A), which can form π-π interactions with aromatic residues. As recently pointed out by Heller et al., 2024, CSPs of IDPs elicited by drug binding can be small enough to fall within the spectral resolution of NMR spectroscopy, therefore making it difficult to unequivocally identify drug-interacting residues. The small magnitude of CSPs may arise because the drug does not have a strong preference for interacting with any residues. Another scenario may be that drug binding induces a conformational shift such as secondary structure formation or even partial folding (De Mol et al., 2016; Iwaya et al., 2020; Robustelli et al., 2022), so CSPs spread from the directly interacting residues to the rest of the IDP, adding to the difficulty in identifying drug-interacting residues.

All-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have presented atomic details in many IDP-drug systems (Jin et al., 2013; Heller et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Basu et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2016; Herrera-Nieto et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022; Mehta and Goyal, 2024). These simulation studies have highlighted the frequent engagement of drug molecules with aromatic residues, particularly in π-π interactions (Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Basu et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2021; Herrera-Nieto et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022; Mehta and Goyal, 2024). MD simulations also revealed the emergence of a compact subpopulation of the N-terminal disordered region of the tumor suppressor protein p53 upon binding the drug epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) (Zhao et al., 2021) and reduced solvent exposure of hydrophobic residues in the 42-residue amyloid-β peptide (Aβ42) upon binding the drug 10074-G5 (Heller et al., 2020). However, MD simulations of IDPs still suffer from the perennial issues of inaccurate force fields and insufficient sampling, which are exacerbated when drug molecules are included. For example, two replicate simulations may identify different drug-interacting residues (Lama et al., 2024).

Here, we present a sequence-based method, DIRseq, as a complement to NMR CSP and MD simulations. This method was motivated by our observation that drug-interacting residues seem to overlap with residues exhibiting elevated transverse relaxation rates (R2) (Qin and Zhou, 2024; Muhammedkutty et al., 2025), as exemplified by the C-terminal 20 residues of α-synuclein (Robustelli et al., 2022). Elevated R2 in IDPs is caused by either local inter-residue interactions or residual secondary structures (Dey et al., 2022). Based on this understanding, we developed a sequence-based method, SeqDYN, to predict R2 of IDPs (Qin and Zhou, 2024). As suggested previously (Muhammedkutty et al., 2025), the propensities of residues to form intramolecular interactions and therefore elevate R2 should be similar to those for forming intermolecular interactions with drug molecules. DIRseq is therefore an adaptation of SeqDYN. DIRseq predictions match well with drug-interacting residues identified by NMR CSP and other methods, including residues L22WK24 and Q52WFT55 in p53 and C-terminal residues in α-synuclein. DIRseq is available as a web server at https://zhougroup-uic.github.io/DIRseq/ and has many applications.

## Results

### Retooling of SeqDYN into DIRseq

SeqDYN (Qin and Zhou, 2024) predicts the $R_{2}$ value of residue n by accumulating a contributing factor $fi;n$ from each residue i:

$$
R_{2}(n)=Υ\prodi=1Nf(i;n)
$$

where N is the total number of residues in the IDP and $Υ$ is a uniform scale parameter. The contributing factor $fi;n$ has an amplitude $q(i)$ that is determined by the amino-acid type of residue i and attenuates with increasing sequence distance, $s=|i-n|$, from residue $n$:

$$
f(i;n)=1+\frac{q(i)−1}{1+bs^{2}}
$$

The 20 $q$ parameters (one for each amino-acid type) and $b$ were trained on the measured $R_{2}$ values for 45 IDPs. The original $q$ values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) show that aromatic (Trp, Tyr, His, and Phe), Arg, and long aliphatic (Ile and Leu) amino acids are interaction-prone and tend to elevate $R_{2}$. (The original SeqDYN also has an option of applying a helix boost; we did not apply this boost here.) We transformed SeqDYN into DIRseq by implementing four changes.

First, we reassigned four $q$ parameters. We lowered the $q$ values of the three long aliphatic amino acids, Leu, Ile, and Met, to the $q$ value of a short aliphatic amino acid, Val, because long aliphatic amino acids primarily participate in hydrophobic interactions, which may be less important for stabilizing the binding of a small molecule in sites largely exposed to water. At the same time, we increased the $q$ value of Asp to be the same as that of Glu, to increase the role of Asp’s electrostatic interactions. Both the downgrade of hydrophobic interactions and the upgrade of electrostatic interactions were motivated by observations on drug binding to α-synuclein in MD simulations by Robustelli et al., 2022. The modified set of $q$ parameters is displayed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

Second, the original $b$ value, 0.0316, corresponds to a correlation half-length, $b^{-1/2}$, of 5.6 residues. Given the small size of drug molecules, we increased the $b$ value to 0.3, corresponding to a correlation half-length of 1.8 residues. That is, we expect a drug molecule to interact with 3–4 residues at a time. Third, the SeqDYN-predicted R2 profile, capturing experimental observations (Klein-Seetharaman et al., 2002), falls off at both termini, because no residues beyond the termini are present to provide a contributing factor to $R_{2}$. However, whereas intra-IDP interactions experience such a terminal effect, IDP-drug interactions do not. To eliminate the terminal effect, we padded the original IDP sequence by a stretch of 12 Gln residues at each terminus. Gln was selected because its $q$ value is at the middle of the 20 $q$ values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).

Lastly, we converted high and low $R_{2}$ values into high and low drug-interacting propensities, respectively, using a sigmoid function

$$
P=\frac{100}{1+e^{−\frac{R_{2}−R_{2th}}{R_{2wd}}}}
$$

where the midpoint $R_{2th}$ and width $R_{2wd}$ of the transition region are determined by the mean ($m$) and standard deviation ($SD$) of the $R_{2}$ values over the entire sequence. Specifically,

$$
R_{2th}=m+s_{1}SD
$$



$$
R_{2wd}=m/s_{2}
$$

We chose $s_{1}$ to be 1.5 and $s_{2}$ to be 14.0. On the DIRseq web server, users can either keep these default values for $b$, $s_{1}$, and $s_{2}$, or enter values of their choice. The source code has been deposited on GitHub under the file name DIRseq.js (https://github.com/hzhou43/DIRseq/; Zhou, 2025). The values of $P$ range from 0 to 100; $P$ = 50 when $R_{2}$ is at the ‘threshold’ value $R_{2th}$. Residues with $P\geq$ 50 are predicted to be drug-interacting, but an isolated residue with $P\geq$ 50 is discarded, as it can be reasonably expected that interactions with at least two consecutive (or nearby) residues are needed to generate sufficient drug binding stability.

### Detailed assessment of DIRseq on four IDPs

Drug-interacting residues in four IDPs or intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) have been thoroughly characterized by NMR CSP. In Figure 1 (left images), we show these IDPs in a single conformation, with DIRseq propensities rendered in a color spectrum (from low in yellow to high in red); predicted drug-interacting residues (i.e. those with $P\geq$ 50) are shown with sidechains in stick. Drug molecules that bind to these IDPs are also displayed in Figure 1 (right images). We display NMR CSPs as blue bars and DIRseq propensities as a red curve in Figure 2. Unless otherwise noted, we use m+1.5 SD as the threshold for identifying drug-interacting residues, for both CSP and DIRseq; this threshold is indicated by a horizontal dashed line in Figure 2. Experimentally identified drug-interacting residues are further indicated by cyan shading. Below, we present a detailed comparison between CSP and DIRseq.

DIRseq predictions are shown as red curves. The ordinate scales are chosen so that the m+1.5 SD threshold for CSP is at the same height as the 50% threshold for DIRseq, indicated by a horizontal dashed line.

The kinase inhibitory domain (residues 22–105) of the cell cycle regulator p27 harbors three aromatic-centered motifs that interact with a group of compounds represented by SJ403 (Figure 1a), as found by Iconaru et al., 2015. These motifs, W60N61, E75WQ77, and Y88Y89 (Figure 2a, cyan shading), are correctly predicted by DIRseq (Figure 2a, portions of the red curve above the 50% threshold). Specifically, the predicted drug-interacting residues are R58KWN61, Y74EWQ77, and Y88Y89 (Figure 1a, left image). Moreover, the DIRseq propensity profile matches well the CSP profile along the sequence (Figure 2a). The two parameters show a very strong correlation, with a Pearson correlation coefficient (r) of 0.82 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).

Iconaru et al. also studied SJ403 binding to a related cell cycle regulator p21. Their CSP data identified the first two corresponding motifs, W49N50 and F63A64, but not the third as drug-interacting residues (Figure 2b, cyan shading). DIRseq correctly predicts both the first two motifs above the 50% threshold and the third motif below the threshold (Figure 2b, red curve; Figure 1b, left image). As noted by Iconaru et al., the p21 counterpart to the p27 third motif F87YY89 is L76YL78; the two Leu residues in p21 are no match for F87 and Y89 in p27. For the DIRseq method, Leu has a lower $q$ value than Tyr and Phe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b). CSP and DIRseq propensity show a strong correlation (r=0.66; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).

NMR CSP revealed two motifs, W23K24 and D49IEQWFT55, in the N-terminal region of p53 as interacting with EGCG (Zhao et al., 2021; Figure 2c, cyan shading). MD simulations supported these drug-binding sites. DIRseq again correctly predicts these two motifs (Figure 2c, red curve). Specifically, the predicted drug-interacting motifs are L22WK24 and E51QWFT55 (Figure 1c, left image). Here also CSP and DIRseq propensity show a strong correlation (r=0.67; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).

Using the m+1.5 SD threshold, CSPs of Robustelli et al., 2022 select residues A124YEMPS129 and Y133QDYE137 of α-synuclein as interacting with the drug Fasudil (Figure 2d, cyan shading). These two C-terminal motifs are also identified by DIRseq, with residues A124YE126 and Y133QDYEP138 above the 50% threshold (Figure 2d, red curve; Figure 1d, left image). There is a moderate correlation (r=0.51; Figure 2—figure supplement 1d) between CSP and DIRseq propensity. Robustelli et al. further characterized the IDP-drug interactions by all-atom simulations, using both full-length α-synuclein and a C-terminal fragment (residues 121–140). Further simulations of the C-terminal fragment binding with additional compounds led to a compound known as Ligand 47 with a somewhat higher affinity than Fasudil. The CSP profiles elicited by Fasudil and Ligand 47 are similar, though with larger amplitudes around Y125 and Y136 by the latter; their correlation coefficient is 0.78 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a). Because DIRseq does not consider any information about the drug molecule, this correlation coefficient between CSPs elicited by two different compounds might be viewed as an upper bound of what can be achieved for the correlation between CSP and DIRseq propensity.

### Dependences of DIRseq prediction accuracies on model parameters

We now use the CSP data of the above four IDPs to assess the dependences of DIRseq prediction accuracies on model parameters (Supplementary file 1B). We use two complementary measures for accuracy: the Pearson correlation between CSP and drug-interacting propensity and the difference between true positive (TP) and false positive (FP). The four IDPs have a total of 31 CSP-identified drug-interacting residues. Recall that DIRseq uses a sigmoid function to convert the $R_{2}$ output of SeqDYN into drug-interacting propensities. Using the original 20 $q$ parameters along with the present values for $b$, $s_{1}$, and $s_{2}$, the predictions are already pretty reasonable: the correlations for the four IDPs range from 0.46 to 0.79 (sum = 2.43) and TP outnumbers FP by 7 residues. Indeed, this initial success was anticipated (Qin and Zhou, 2024; Muhammedkutty et al., 2025) and validated the premise of DIRseq, i.e., intra-IDP interactions that elevate $R_{2}$ also tend to mediate drug interactions. As stated above, we tweaked 4 of the 20 $q$ parameters to arrive at the final DIRseq; now the r sum increases to 2.66 and TP – FP increases to 15.

Examining the four $q$ parameter changes one at a time, the downgrade of $q$ for Leu increases both r sum (to 2.53) and TP – FP (to 16) relative to the counterparts with the original SeqDYN $q$ parameters. In comparison, the downgrade of $q$ for Ile does not affect r sum and yields a small increase in TP – FP (to 10), the upgrade of $q$ for Asp yields small increases in both r sum (to 2.52) and TP – FP (to 8), but the downgrade of $q$ for Met actually decreases both r sum (to 2.37) and TP – FP (to 6). The latter result shows that we made these parameter tweaks not solely for increasing accuracy but for physical reasons, i.e., to reduce the role of hydrophobic interactions but elevate the role of electrostatic interactions in IDP-drug binding, as suggested by MD simulations.

We also tested alternative models for $q$ parameters. Given the prominence of aromatic amino acids in drug binding as revealed by CSP, we wondered how a model that solely emphasizes aromatic amino acids would perform. To that end, we tested a model with only two different $q$ values for the 20 amino acids: a high value (same as that of Trp in SeqDYN) for all three aromatic amino acids (Trp, Tyr, and Phe) and a low value (same as that of Gly in SeqDYN) for all other amino acids. This is similar to a sticker-spacer model for simulating liquid-liquid phase separation (Martin et al., 2020). This aromatic model achieves the same r sum, 2.66, as DIRseq, but its FP outnumbers its TP, such that TP – FP = –1. Tesei and Lindorff-Larsen, 2022 parameterized a coarse-grained force field to simulate liquid-liquid phase separation. Their $\lambda$ ‘stickiness’ parameters have a good correlation with the SeqDYN original $q$ parameters (Zhou et al., 2024). We replaced the $q$ parameters by these $\lambda$ parameters (after scaling to the same numerical range as the $q$ parameters); the resulting model has both a low r sum (1.21) and a low TP – FP (–21). This outcome suggests that, unlike liquid-liquid phase separation where stickiness is the main drive, drug binding is more selective in the type of intermolecular interactions. Lastly, we tested a model where an average hydropathy scale (compiled by Tesei et al., 2021) was used in place of the $q$ parameters; the resulting model has very little predictive value (r sum = 0.44 and TP – FP = –20). This last outcome is in line with our downgrade of hydrophobic interactions in DIRseq. The test results from all these alternative models indicate that the $q$ parameters in the final DIRseq model capture the appropriate balance among aromatic, electrostatic, and hydrophobic interactions in IDP-drug binding.

In addition to the 20 $q$ parameters, DIRseq has 3 other parameters. The $b$ parameter determines the number of residues that simultaneously interact with a drug molecule. In Supplementary file 1, we list the performance measures when $b$ is varied. These results show that our final choice, 0.3, for $b$ is optimal for both r sum and TP – FP. The corresponding number of residues, 3–4, that simultaneously interact with a drug molecule fits with the narrow range of drug molecule sizes in the present study (Supplementary file 1A; molecular weights: 360±130 Da). The last two parameters, $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$, are in the sigmoid function that converts the $R_{2}$ output into drug-interacting propensities. $s_{1}$ sets the $R_{2}$ threshold for labeling a residue as drug-interacting. Again, our final choice, corresponding to m+1.5 SD for the threshold, achieves an optimum for r sum and TP – FP. A lower threshold leads to a high FP and also a slight deterioration in r sum, whereas a higher threshold leads to a low FP and possibly a minuscule improvement in r sum. $s_{2}$ controls the sharpness of the sigmoid function in the transition region and affects r sum but not TP – FP. r sum increases with increasing $s_{2}$; we chose an $s_{2}$ value, where r sum is nearly at the saturation level.

### DIRseq as a complement to CSP for assigning drug-interacting residues

After assessing the achievable accuracy of DIRseq, we now consider an application: its combination with CSP to make robust assignments of drug-interacting residues. We note that the above CSP-identified drug-interacting motifs are all anchored on one or more aromatic residues, and this feature likely contributes to the good performance of DIRseq. When a clear ‘aromatic signal’ is not present, CSP or DIRseq alone may not be able to conclusively identify drug-interacting residues. However, a consensus identification by CSP and DIRseq may be reliable. MD simulations have played such a complementary role to CSP in several studies (Zhao et al., 2021; Robustelli et al., 2022; Basu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2022).

De Mol et al., 2016 reported the CSPs of an IDR called AF-1* (residues 142–448) in the androgen receptor elicited by EPI-001 and its stereoisomers, including EPI-002; small but reproducible CSPs were found in three subregions, R1 (residues 341–371), R2 (residues 391–414), and R3 (residues 426–446). Conversely, AF-1* caused changes in the 1H NMR spectrum of EPI-001, but the individual peptides corresponding to R1, R2, and R3 did not, suggesting that, rather than separately interacting with the three subregions, EPI-001 induces a partial folding of the three subregions. MD simulations captured the partial folding of the R2-R3 fragment (residues 391–446) induced by EPI-002 and underscored the importance of aromatic residues in drug binding (Zhu et al., 2022). Basu et al., 2023 reported the CSPs of the transactivation unit 5 (Tau-5*, residues 336–448) in AF-1* by EPI-001 and a more potent variant, 1aa (Figure 3a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b). The contact probabilities of the R2-R3 fragment with 1aa in MD simulations reaffirmed the importance of aromatic residues.

![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/107470/elife-107470-fig3-v1.jpg)

**Figure 3.:** (a) Tau-5*. (b) NS5A-D2D3. (c) β2 microglobulin. Display items in panels (a, b) have the same meanings as in Figure 2, except that cyan shading indicates consensus identification; in panel (c), vertical lines indicate mutation sites.

De Mol et al., 2016 and Basu et al., 2023 were careful not to name any drug-interacting residues based on CSPs. In Figure 3a, we compare the 1aa-elicited CSPs and DIRseq propensities of Tau-5*. In agreement with both NMR studies, DIRseq identifies drug-interacting residues in the middle of each of R1-R3: R360DYY363, A396WAA399, and W433H434. In addition, the latter two motifs showed the highest drug-contact probabilities in separate MD simulations of the R2-R3 fragment (Basu et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2022). For the R2 and R3 subregions, CSPs above the m+1.5 SD threshold are observed at residues downstream of the DIRseq identifications, so we propose to expand the drug-interacting motifs to A396WAAAAAQ403 and W433HTLF437. The three putative drug-interacting motifs are indicated as cyan shading in Figure 3a.

Heller et al., 2024 used 19F transverse relaxation measurements to determine the binding affinity of the disordered domains 2 and 3 of the hepatitis C virus NS5A protein (NS5A-D2D3, residues 247–466) for 5-fluorindole. They also measured 1H-15N CSPs at two ligand concentrations but described them as ‘nearly undetectable’ (Figure 3b). We speculate that the small CSPs may be due to the small size of the ligand, making it difficult to interact with multiple residues simultaneously and thus achieve sufficient binding stability. In any event, CSPs above the m+1.5 SD threshold were largely isolated (and thus appeared to be random), and there was not much overlap between residues having these above-the-threshold CSPs at the two ligand concentrations. The one exception is a motif around W312, which had above-the-threshold CSPs at both ligand concentrations, and nearby residues A308 and A313 also had above-the-threshold CSPs at one of the ligand concentrations. DIRseq predicts the motif P310AWARPD316 as drug-interacting residues. We propose the expanded motif, A308LPAWARPD316, as residues interacting with 5-fluorindole (Figure 3b, cyan shading). DIRseq also predicts two more motifs, E323SWRRPDY330 and R352RRR355, as drug-interacting residues, which remain to be tested.

The fibrillation of acid-denatured β2 microglobulin is inhibited by rifamycin SV (Woods et al., 2011). An aromatic-rich motif, W60SFYLLYYTEF70, was implicated in the nucleation of fibrillation and also involved in ligand binding, as a triple mutation, F62A/Y63A/Y67A, significantly weakened binding. Low intensities of NMR peaks from residues 58–79 (possibly due to the formation of residual structures) prevented the measurement of CSPs. DIRseq predicts D59WSFY63 as drug-interacting residues. Combined with the mutational data of Woods et al., 2011, we propose the expanded motif, D59WSFYLLYY67, as the major drug-binding site (Figure 3c, cyan shading). DIRseq also predicts an additional motif, K94WDR97, as drug-interacting residues.

The aggregation of human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP; 37 residues) is inhibited by the small molecule YX-I-1 (Xu et al., 2022). CSPs elicited by this molecule were small (Figure 4a). In addition, CSPs of short IDPs may not exhibit strong disparities because amino acids may be too well mixed along the sequence or drug binding may induce a conformational shift. We thus reduce the threshold for identifying drug-interacting residues to m+1.0 SD when the number of residues is ≤50. With this threshold, three residues are identified by CSP as drug-interacting residues: R11 and V17H18. In comparison, DIRseq identifies T9QRLA13 and F15 as drug-interacting residues, which partially overlap with the CSP identifications. Combining the two types of data, we propose T9QRLANFLVH18 as the primary drug-binding site (Figure 4a, cyan shading). We note that this motif is also prone to α-helix formation (Apostolidou et al., 2008).

**Figure 4.:** (a) hIAPP. (b) Aβ42. (c) c-Myc. Display items have the same meanings as in Figure 2, but with the following exceptions. (1) In panel (b), vertical lines indicate residues with prominent CSPs; those accompanied by NMR peak broadening have their vertical lines in dark color. (2) In panel (c), three CSP-identified drug-interacting regions are indicated by cyan, olive, and yellow shading. (3) The threshold for identifying drug-interacting residues is lowered to m+1.0 SD.

Ono et al., 2012 acquired 1H-15N heteronuclear single quantum coherence spectra of the 42-residue amyloid-β (Aβ42) in the absence and presence of the oligomerization-blocking compound myricetin. CSPs were not calculated, but chemical shift movements were most pronounced at R5, V12H13, K16LVFFAED23, and I31I32 (vertical lines in Figure 4b). In addition, NMR cross peaks suffered broadening upon ligand binding at four of these residues: R5, V12, K16, and V18 (dark vertical lines in Figure 4b), implicating elevated probabilities of ligand interactions. DIRseq predicts E3FRH6 and H13H14 as drug-interacting residues. Combined with the NMR data, we propose E3FRH6 and V12HHQKLV18 as the primary ligand-binding sites (Figure 4b, cyan shading). Aβ42 CSPs elicited by several other compounds were also widely distributed over the sequence, such that Iwaya et al., 2020 ‘failed to identify’ drug-interacting residues, implicating a conformational shift.

Hammoudeh et al., 2009 identified three distinct drug binding sites in a C-terminal IDR (residues 363–412) of the oncoprotein c-Myc. This region is disordered on its own but forms a helix-loop-helix structure upon heterodimerization with Max. These authors measured the CSPs of three overlapping fragments (residues 363–381, 370–409, and 402–412), each in the presence of a single compound and of the full IDR in the presence of all three compounds. Using 20 parts per billion (ppb) as the threshold, Hammoudeh et al. named residues R366RNELKRSFF375, F375ALRDQIPELE385, and Y402ILSVQAE409 as the binding sites for 10074-G5, 10074-A4, and 10058-F4, respectively. We present their CSP data for the full IDR in Figure 4c. Using the m+1.0 SD threshold, only six residues are identified as drug-interacting residues: R367, L370, F374F375, A399, and S405. DIRseq predicts two motifs, E363RQRR367 and K371RSFFA376, that overlap with the first two sites identified by CSP; a third motif, K397KATAY402, that corresponds to the third CSP-identified site has moderate drug-interacting propensities. Combining CSP and DIRseq, we revise the three drug-binding sites to be E363RQRRNELKRSFF375, S373FFALRDQI381, and K397KATAYILS405 (Figure 4c, cyan, olive, and yellow shading, respectively). In addition to 10074-G5, 10074-A4, and 10058-F4, many compounds bind to these three sites (Yu et al., 2016; Han et al., 2019; Shirey et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024).

## Discussion

We have presented the first sequence-based method, DIRseq, to predict drug-interacting residues of IDPs. Assessment against NMR CSP demonstrates the accuracy of DIRseq. Drug-binding motifs are anchored on one or more aromatic residues for forming π-π interactions with drug-like molecules that are rich in aromatic groups. The success of DIRseq comes without any specific information on the drug molecules, suggesting that IDPs may have a relatively simple sequence code for drug binding.

The notion that drug-interacting residues may be agnostic to the molecular details of drug compounds is supported by the fact that the same drug can bind to different IDPs. For example, in addition to p53 (Zhao et al., 2021; Figure 2c), the polyphenol EGCG also binds to many other IDPs, including α-synuclein (Ehrnhoefer et al., 2008), hIAPP (Young et al., 2014; Meng et al., 2010), Aβ40 (Ahmed et al., 2017) and Aβ42 (Ehrnhoefer et al., 2008), tau (Wobst et al., 2015), and merozoite surface protein 2 (Chandrashekaran et al., 2010). Likewise, 10074-G5 binds to c-Myc (Hammoudeh et al., 2009; Figure 4c) but also to Aβ42 (Heller et al., 2020). On the other hand, c-Myc represents a case where different compounds bind to distinct sites on a single IDP (Hammoudeh et al., 2009). A related example is presented by p27, where SJ403 typifies a group of compounds that share the same three binding sites (Figure 2a). Another group of compounds, typified by SJ710, binds only to the third site. Chemically, the presence of nitrogen atoms in the rings of SJ403 enhances its aromaticity and thus strengthens π-π interactions; in addition, the electronegative groups of SJ403 project into different directions, making it less restricted when forming electrostatic interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). These features may explain why SJ403 can bind to all three sites, whereas SJ710 can bind only to the third site, F87YYR90, where three consecutive aromatic residues followed by a basic residue ensure that SJ710 can form both π-π and electrostatic interactions. When more data for multiple drugs binding to a single IDP becomes available, it will be important to use such data to train the next generation of DIRseq where the parameters are drug-specific. As a simple example, the number of residues that can simultaneously bind a drug molecule may grow with the latter’s size; this dependence can be modeled by making the parameter $b$ dependent on drug molecule size. The drug molecules studied in the present work have molecular weights of 360±130 Da and thus span a relatively narrow size range.

We have illustrated the combination of DIRseq with NMR CSP to make robust identifications of drug-binding sites in IDPs. Indeed, CSP, MD simulations, and DIRseq are three orthogonal approaches that have great potential in complementing each other, not only for identifying drug-binding sites but also for elucidating the roles of amino acids, their sequence context, and different types of noncovalent interactions in forming such sites. DIRseq offers fast speed and a simple, direct link between sequence motif and propensity for drug binding.

Another application of DIRseq is to define IDP fragments for in-depth study by MD simulations, as shorter constructs both enable the use of a smaller simulation box and reduce the size of the conformational space. For example, based on CSP data and initial MD simulations of full-length α-synuclein, Robustelli et al., 2022 chose a 20-residue C-terminal fragment for simulations of binding with additional compounds, leading to the identification of Ligand 47 as a stronger binder than the original Fasudil. Similarly, based on CSP data from longer constructs of the androgen receptor, both Zhu et al., 2022 and Basu et al., 2023 chose the 56-residue R2-R3 fragment for MD simulations of drug binding. DIRseq can now play a similar role in selecting fragments for MD simulations when CSP data are unavailable. Longer constructs may also present challenges such as resonance assignments to NMR experiments, so well-chosen fragments guided by DIRseq can also benefit NMR studies.

Lastly, virtual screening has been conducted against conformational ensembles of IDPs (Ruan et al., 2021; Dhar et al., 2025); drug-binding sites predicted by DIRseq can be used to guide such screening. As a simple illustration, we present poses of EGCG generated by screening against the two DIRseq-predicted binding sites in p53 in Figure 5. As IDPs sample a vast conformational space, knowledge of the binding site can drastically reduce the computational cost. The subset of conformations that generate high docking scores for a given drug at the known site can also provide insight into the mechanism of drug action.

## Methods

The sequences of the IDP studied here and the drugs that bind to them are listed in Supplementary file 1A. All DIRseq predictions were obtained using the web server at https://zhougroup-uic.github.io/DIRseq/. Conformations of IDPs were generated using the TraDES method (Feldman and Hogue, 2002).

Docking of EGCG onto p53 was performed via the SwissDock web server at https://www.swissdock.ch/ (Bugnon et al., 2024) utilizing the Autodock Vina docking engine (Eberhardt et al., 2021). The SMILES string for EGCG from PubChem (CID 65064) and several conformations of p53 were used as input. A cubic region (13–20 Å in side length) around the center of each drug-interacting residue was selected for docking.

Summary:

The authors developed a sequence-based method to predict drug-interacting residues in IDP, based on their recent work, to predict the transverse relaxation rates (R2) of IDP trained on 45 IDP sequences and their corresponding R2 values. The discovery is that the IDPs interact with drugs mostly using aromatic residues that are easy to understand, as most drugs contain aromatic rings. They validated the method using several case studies, and the predictions are in accordance with chemical shift perturbations and MD simulations. The location of the predicted residues serves as a starting point for ligand optimization.

Strengths:

This work provides the first sequence-based prediction method to identify potential drug-interacting residues in IDP. The validity of the method is supported by case studies. It is easy to use, and no time-consuming MD simulations and NMR studies are needed.

Weaknesses:

The method does not depend on the information of binding compounds, which may give general features of IDP-drug binding. However, due to the size and chemical structures of the compounds (for example, how many aromatic rings), the number of interacting residues varies, which is not considered in this work. Lacking specific information may restrict its application in compound optimization, aiming to derive specific and potent binding compounds.

results.result: DIRseq is a sequence-based method adapted from SeqDYN to predict drug-interacting residues in IDPs. The method was developed by implementing four changes to SeqDYN, including reassigning q parameters to downgrade hydrophobic interactions and upgrade electrostatic interactions, adjusting the correlation half-length parameter b to expect 3-4 residues to interact with a drug molecule simultaneously, eliminating terminal effects by padding sequences with Gln residues, and converting R2 values to drug-interacting propensities using a sigmoid function.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17, C25, C29, C32, C34-C35 collectively describe the methodological development of DIRseq from SeqDYN. The modifications are clearly stated and justified based on physical reasoning (C29) and prior observations (C13, C16). The parameter choices are explained with logical rationale (C32, C34, C35), providing a coherent methodological framework.

results.result: DIRseq correctly predicts three aromatic-centered drug-interacting motifs in p27 (R58KWN61, Y74EWQ77, and Y88Y89) that bind to SJ403, showing very strong correlation (r=0.82) with NMR CSP data.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 demonstrate strong agreement between DIRseq predictions and experimental CSP data for p27. The specific motifs are identified (C41-C43), visual agreement is shown (C44), and quantitative correlation is high (C45, r=0.82). This represents successful validation of the method on a well-characterized system.

results.result: DIRseq correctly predicts drug-interacting residues in p21, identifying the first two motifs (W49N50 and F63A64) above the 50% threshold and the third motif below threshold, consistent with CSP data showing weaker binding at the third site due to amino acid composition differences from p27.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 show DIRseq correctly distinguishes between strong and weak binding sites in p21. The method predicts the first two motifs above threshold and third below (C47), consistent with CSP observations (C46). The amino acid composition explanation (C48-C49) provides mechanistic insight. Strong correlation (r=0.66, C51) supports the predictions.

results.result: DIRseq correctly predicts two drug-interacting motifs in p53 (L22WK24 and E51QWFT55) that bind EGCG, showing strong correlation (r=0.67) with NMR CSP data and agreement with MD simulation results.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 demonstrate successful DIRseq prediction for p53-EGCG binding. The two motifs are identified by both CSP (C52) and DIRseq (C54-C55), with MD simulation support (C53). The strong correlation (r=0.67, C56) validates the predictions. This represents independent validation on a different IDP-drug system.

results.result: DIRseq identifies C-terminal drug-interacting residues in α-synuclein (A124YE126 and Y133QDYEP138) binding to Fasudil, showing moderate correlation (r=0.51) with CSP data. The correlation between CSPs elicited by two different compounds (Fasudil and Ligand 47, r=0.78) may represent an upper bound for CSP-DIRseq correlation since DIRseq does not use drug-specific information.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 show DIRseq successfully identifies drug-binding regions in α-synuclein with moderate correlation (C59). The comparison between two different ligands (C62-C63) provides important context for interpreting the CSP-DIRseq correlation (C64), suggesting the method performs reasonably well given its sequence-only approach. The MD simulation context (C60-C61) adds validation.

results.result: Parameter optimization shows that DIRseq's final parameters (b=0.3, s1=m+1.5 SD) achieve optimal performance. Alternative models based solely on aromatic residues or stickiness parameters perform poorly, indicating that drug binding requires a balanced consideration of aromatic, electrostatic, and hydrophobic interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C73, C77-C80 demonstrate systematic parameter optimization and comparison with alternative models. The aromatic-only model has poor TP-FP balance (C71), the stickiness model fails (C73), and the final parameter choices are justified (C77-C80). This provides evidence that the method captures appropriate physical interactions for drug binding.

results.result: CSP-identified drug-interacting motifs in the four well-characterized IDPs are all anchored on aromatic residues, which likely contributes to DIRseq's good performance. When clear aromatic signals are absent, consensus identification by CSP and DIRseq may be more reliable than either method alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 provide important insights into the method's scope and limitations. The observation about aromatic anchoring (C82-C83) is supported by the data from four IDPs. The speculation about combining methods (C84-C85) is reasonable and supported by examples from prior work (C86). This appropriately qualifies the method's applicability.

results.result: DIRseq identifies drug-interacting residues in Tau-5* of the androgen receptor (R360DYY363, A396WAA399, W433H434) that were not definitively assigned by CSP alone due to small signal amplitudes. The predictions are supported by MD simulations showing high drug-contact probabilities for the latter two motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C98 demonstrate DIRseq's utility in cases where CSP data are ambiguous. The NMR studies (C87-C95) identified regions but did not assign specific residues, while DIRseq makes specific predictions (C96) that are supported by MD simulations (C97). The proposed expanded motifs (C98) represent reasonable consensus assignments combining multiple data sources.

results.result: For NS5A-D2D3 binding to 5-fluorindole, where CSPs were nearly undetectable, DIRseq predicts the motif P310AWARPD316 as drug-interacting residues. An expanded motif A308LPAWARPD316 is proposed based on combining CSP and DIRseq data, and two additional motifs are predicted but remain to be tested.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 present predictions for a challenging case with very weak CSP signals (C100). While DIRseq makes specific predictions (C102, C104), the experimental validation is limited due to the weak CSP data. The speculation about ligand size (C101) is reasonable but unproven. The proposed motifs (C103) require experimental validation to be considered supported.

results.result: For β2 microglobulin binding to rifamycin SV, DIRseq predicts D59WSFY63 as drug-interacting residues. Combined with mutational data showing that F62A/Y63A/Y67A weakens binding, the major drug-binding site is proposed to be D59WSFYLLYY67, with an additional predicted motif K94WDR97.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C111 show successful integration of DIRseq predictions with mutational data. The DIRseq prediction (C109) overlaps with the mutationally-defined binding region (C106-C107), and CSP measurements were prevented by technical issues (C108). The proposed expanded motif (C110) represents a reasonable consensus combining computational and experimental data.

results.result: For the short IDP hIAPP (37 residues) binding to YX-I-1, DIRseq identifies T9QRLA13 and F15 as drug-interacting residues, which partially overlap with CSP identifications (R11, V17H18) using a lowered threshold (m+1.0 SD). The proposed primary binding site T9QRLANFLVH18 is also prone to α-helix formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C118 demonstrate DIRseq application to a short IDP with small CSPs (C113). The methodological adjustment for short sequences (C114) is reasonable. The partial overlap between DIRseq (C116) and CSP (C115) predictions supports the consensus assignment (C117). The connection to helix propensity (C118) provides additional structural context.

results.result: For Aβ42 binding to myricetin, DIRseq predicts E3FRH6 and H13H14 as drug-interacting residues. Combined with NMR data showing prominent chemical shift movements and peak broadening at specific residues, the primary ligand-binding sites are proposed to be E3FRH6 and V12HHQKLV18.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C123 show successful integration of DIRseq with qualitative NMR data. While CSPs were not calculated (C120), chemical shift movements and peak broadening (C121) provide experimental support. The DIRseq predictions (C122) overlap with the NMR observations, and the proposed binding sites (C123) represent reasonable consensus assignments.

results.result: For c-Myc binding to multiple compounds, DIRseq predicts two motifs (E363RQRR367 and K371RSFFA376) that overlap with CSP-identified sites, and a third motif (K397KATAY402) with moderate propensities. Combining CSP and DIRseq data, three revised drug-binding sites are proposed: E363RQRRNELKRSFF375, S373FFALRDQI381, and K397KATAYILS405.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C133 demonstrate DIRseq's utility for a complex case with multiple binding sites and compounds. The reanalysis of CSP data with a more stringent threshold (C129) is methodologically sound. DIRseq predictions (C130-C131) show good agreement with CSP for two sites and moderate agreement for the third. The revised binding sites (C132) represent reasonable consensus assignments supported by multiple compounds (C133).

results.result: DIRseq is the first sequence-based method to predict drug-interacting residues of IDPs. Assessment against NMR CSP demonstrates its accuracy. Drug-binding motifs are anchored on aromatic residues for π-π interactions, and the method's success without drug-specific information suggests IDPs may have a relatively simple sequence code for drug binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C138 summarize the main findings. The novelty claim (C134) appears valid based on the literature cited. The accuracy assessment (C135) is supported by the correlation data from multiple IDPs. The mechanistic insights about aromatic anchoring (C136) are well-supported. The speculation about a simple sequence code (C138) is reasonable given the method's success (C137).

results.result: The same drug can bind to different IDPs (e.g., EGCG binds to multiple IDPs, 10074-G5 binds to c-Myc and Aβ42), while different compounds can bind to distinct sites on a single IDP (e.g., c-Myc, p27). Chemical properties of compounds (e.g., aromaticity, electronegative group orientation in SJ403) may explain binding site selectivity. Future development should incorporate drug-specific parameters when more data become available.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C149 provide important context about drug-IDP binding promiscuity and specificity. The examples of cross-binding (C140-C141) and site-specific binding (C142-C144) are well-documented in the cited literature. The chemical reasoning about SJ403 vs SJ710 (C145-C148) is sound. The suggestion for future development (C149) is reasonable and appropriately speculative.

results.result: DIRseq offers fast speed and a direct link between sequence and drug-binding propensity. The method can be used to define IDP fragments for in-depth MD simulations and NMR studies, as shorter constructs reduce computational cost and experimental challenges. CSP, MD simulations, and DIRseq are orthogonal approaches with great potential to complement each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C160 discuss practical applications and limitations. The narrow drug size range (C151) is acknowledged. The proposed applications for fragment selection (C154, C158, C160) are reasonable and supported by examples from prior work (C156-C157). The advantages of DIRseq (C153) are clear. The statement about complementary approaches (C152) is well-justified by the examples presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Drug-binding sites predicted by DIRseq can guide virtual screening against IDP conformational ensembles, drastically reducing computational cost. The subset of conformations generating high docking scores at known sites can provide insight into drug action mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C164 propose applications for virtual screening. While virtual screening against IDPs has been conducted (C161), the utility of DIRseq for guiding such screening (C162) remains speculative and untested. The logical reasoning about computational cost reduction (C163) and mechanistic insights (C164) is sound, but experimental validation is needed.

results.result: IDPs are recognized drug targets, with NMR CSP as the primary experimental method for identifying drug-interacting residues. Aromatic residues are frequently involved in drug binding through π-π interactions with aromatic-rich drug molecules. MD simulations provide atomic details but suffer from force field inaccuracies and sampling limitations. CSPs can be small and difficult to interpret due to spectral resolution limits or conformational changes upon binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 establish the scientific context and motivation for the study. These claims are well-supported by extensive citations to published literature (C1-C10, C12) and established knowledge about MD simulation limitations (C11). This background appropriately frames the need for the DIRseq method.

results.result: Drug-interacting residues overlap with residues exhibiting elevated R2 values, which are caused by local inter-residue interactions or residual secondary structures. This observation motivated the development of DIRseq from SeqDYN, based on the premise that propensities for intramolecular interactions (elevating R2) should be similar to those for intermolecular interactions with drugs.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 establish the conceptual foundation for DIRseq. The observation about R2 overlap (C13) is supported by citations. The mechanistic understanding of elevated R2 (C14) and the development of SeqDYN (C15) provide the basis for the adaptation. The key premise (C16) is reasonable and forms the logical foundation for the method.

results.result: IDP conformations were generated using the TraDES method, and docking of EGCG onto p53 was performed using SwissDock with Autodock Vina.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C166 describe computational methods used for generating example docking poses. These are standard, well-established methods appropriately cited. The docking results are presented as illustrations rather than primary validation data.

results.result: DIRseq is an adaptation of SeqDYN, created by implementing four changes: downgrading hydrophobic interactions, upgrading electrostatic interactions, adjusting the correlation half-length parameter (b) to reflect that drug molecules interact with 3–4 residues at a time, and eliminating the terminal effect by padding sequences with 12 Gln residues at each terminus.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the method builds on the authors' previous work (SeqDYN) and accept the modifications made. The editor notes 'the method builds on the authors' previous work' without raising concerns about the methodological adaptations.

results.result: DIRseq correctly predicts three aromatic-centered motifs in p27 (W60N61, E75WQ77, Y88Y89) that interact with SJ403, with the DIRseq propensity profile matching the CSP profile (Pearson r=0.82).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this validation case. The editor states 'validation was done on a total of 10 IDPs at varying depths' and notes 'findings have solid support through examples underscoring the role of aromatic interactions,' implicitly accepting the p27 results as part of the validation set.

results.result: DIRseq correctly predicts the first two motifs in p21 (W49N50, F63A64) above the 50% threshold and the third motif below threshold, consistent with CSP data showing only the first two motifs as drug-interacting residues (r=0.66). The difference is explained by sequence composition: p21's L76YL78 lacks the aromatic residues present in p27's corresponding F87YY89 motif.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the validation set. The editor's statement about validation across 10 IDPs and the emphasis on aromatic interactions implicitly supports these findings comparing p27 and p21.

results.result: DIRseq correctly predicts two drug-binding motifs in p53 (L22WK24 and E51QWFT55) that interact with EGCG, matching NMR CSP data (W23K24 and D49IEQWFT55) and supported by MD simulations (r=0.67).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this validation case. The editor notes validation across multiple IDPs and that findings are supported by examples. No concerns are raised about the p53 predictions or their agreement with experimental data.

results.result: DIRseq identifies C-terminal motifs in α-synuclein (A124YE126 and Y133QDYEP138) as drug-interacting residues for Fasudil, showing moderate correlation with CSP (r=0.51). The correlation between CSPs elicited by two different compounds (Fasudil and Ligand 47, r=0.78) represents an upper bound for CSP-DIRseq correlation since DIRseq does not consider drug-specific information.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this validation case and the interpretation of correlation limits. The editor acknowledges validation across 10 IDPs. One reviewer notes 'the method does not depend on the information of binding compounds' as a limitation but does not challenge the α-synuclein results themselves.

results.result: Parameter optimization shows that an aromatic-only model achieves the same correlation sum (2.66) as DIRseq but with more false positives (TP–FP = –1), while DIRseq's optimized parameters (correlation half-length b corresponding to 3–4 residues, threshold at m+1.5 SD) achieve optimal performance. This suggests drug binding is more selective than liquid-liquid phase separation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the parameter optimization and the distinction from simpler models. The editor notes the method involves 'ad hoc modifications' but does not challenge the optimization results. The finding that aromatic interactions alone are insufficient is consistent with reviewer emphasis on the importance of aromatic residues.

results.result: CSP-identified drug-interacting motifs in the four primary IDPs (p27, p21, p53, α-synuclein) are all anchored on aromatic residues, which likely contributes to DIRseq's good performance. When clear aromatic signals are absent, consensus identification by CSP and DIRseq may be more reliable than either method alone.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support the role of aromatic interactions. The editor explicitly states 'findings have solid support through examples underscoring the role of aromatic interactions.' One reviewer notes 'the discovery is that the IDPs interact with drugs mostly using aromatic residues that are easy to understand, as most drugs contain aromatic rings.'

results.result: For the androgen receptor Tau-5* fragment, DIRseq identifies drug-interacting residues in three subregions (R360DYY363, A396WAA399, W433H434), consistent with CSP data showing small but reproducible perturbations in R1, R2, and R3. MD simulations support the importance of aromatic residues and show A396WAA399 and W433H434 have highest drug-contact probabilities. The proposed expanded motifs are A396WAAAAAQ403 and W433HTLF437.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the validation set. The editor's statement about validation across 10 IDPs and the complementary role of MD simulations implicitly supports these findings. The integration of CSP, DIRseq, and MD simulation data is consistent with reviewer emphasis on multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: For NS5A-D2D3, DIRseq predicts motifs P310AWARPD316, E323SWRRPDY330, and R352RRR355 as drug-interacting residues for 5-fluorindole. CSPs were 'nearly undetectable,' possibly due to the small ligand size. The proposed expanded motif for the first site is A308LPAWARPD316.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly discuss this case. The editor notes 'predicted binding sites remain coarse' and validation was done 'at varying depths,' suggesting some cases have weaker support. The speculation about small CSPs due to ligand size and the untested additional motifs indicate uncertainty about these predictions.

results.result: For β2 microglobulin, DIRseq predicts D59WSFY63 and K94WDR97 as drug-interacting residues for rifamycin SV. Combined with mutational data showing F62A/Y63A/Y67A weakens binding, the proposed major drug-binding site is D59WSFYLLYY67. CSP measurement was prevented by low NMR peak intensities in residues 58–79.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the validation set. The integration of DIRseq predictions with mutational data provides orthogonal support. The editor's statement about validation across 10 IDPs includes this case, and the use of mutational data aligns with reviewer emphasis on multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: For hIAPP (37 residues), DIRseq identifies T9QRLA13 and F15 as drug-interacting residues for YX-I-1, partially overlapping with CSP identifications (R11, V17H18) using a reduced threshold (m+1.0 SD for sequences ≤50 residues). The proposed primary drug-binding site is T9QRLANFLVH18, which is also prone to α-helix formation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the validation set. The editor's statement about validation across 10 IDPs includes this case. The methodological adjustment for short sequences (reduced threshold) is not challenged, and the partial overlap between DIRseq and CSP is consistent with the overall validation approach.

results.result: For Aβ42, DIRseq predicts E3FRH6 and H13H14 as drug-interacting residues for myricetin. Combined with NMR data showing chemical shift movements and peak broadening at R5, V12H13, K16LVFFAED23, and I31I32, the proposed primary ligand-binding sites are E3FRH6 and V12HHQKLV18.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the validation set. The editor's statement about validation across 10 IDPs includes this case. The integration of DIRseq predictions with NMR chemical shift movements and peak broadening provides multiple lines of evidence consistent with reviewer emphasis.

results.result: For c-Myc, DIRseq predicts two motifs (E363RQRR367 and K371RSFFA376) that overlap with CSP-identified sites, and a third motif (K397KATAY402) with moderate propensities. Reanalysis using m+1.0 SD threshold identifies only six residues by CSP. The revised three drug-binding sites are E363RQRRNELKRSFF375, S373FFALRDQI381, and K397KATAYILS405, which bind multiple compounds.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as part of the validation set. The editor's statement about validation across 10 IDPs includes this case. The reanalysis of CSP data and integration with DIRseq predictions demonstrates the complementary value of the methods, consistent with reviewer emphasis on multiple approaches.

results.result: DIRseq is the first sequence-based method to predict drug-interacting residues of IDPs, with accuracy demonstrated by assessment against NMR CSP. Drug-binding motifs are anchored on aromatic residues for π-π interactions with aromatic-rich drug molecules. The success without drug-specific information suggests IDPs may have a relatively simple sequence code for drug binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly support the novelty and validation of the method. The editor states this is an 'important study' presenting 'a sequence-based method for predicting drug-interacting residues' with 'solid support.' One reviewer notes 'this work provides the first sequence-based prediction method' and 'the validity of the method is supported by case studies.' The role of aromatic interactions is emphasized by all reviewers.

results.result: The same drug can bind to different IDPs (e.g., EGCG binds to p53, α-synuclein, hIAPP, Aβ40, Aβ42, tau, and merozoite surface protein 2; 10074-G5 binds to c-Myc and Aβ42), while different compounds can bind to distinct sites on a single IDP (e.g., c-Myc has three sites; p27 has compounds like SJ403 binding all three sites vs. SJ710 binding only the third site F87YYR90). Chemical properties (nitrogen atoms enhancing aromaticity, electronegative group orientation) may explain binding selectivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these observations about promiscuity and selectivity. One reviewer notes 'the method does not depend on the information of binding compounds, which may give general features of IDP-drug binding' and acknowledges that 'due to the size and chemical structures of the compounds... the number of interacting residues varies,' implicitly accepting the described patterns while noting limitations.

results.result: DIRseq has multiple applications: it offers fast speed and direct sequence-to-propensity links; can define IDP fragments for MD simulations (as done by Robustelli et al. for α-synuclein and by Zhu et al. and Basu et al. for androgen receptor); can guide NMR studies by selecting well-chosen fragments; and can guide virtual screening against IDP conformational ensembles, reducing computational cost. CSP, MD simulations, and DIRseq are orthogonal approaches with great potential to complement each other.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support the practical applications and complementary nature of methods. The editor notes the method 'is poised to benefit this emerging field.' One reviewer states 'it is easy to use, and no time-consuming MD simulations and NMR studies are needed' and notes 'the location of the predicted residues serves as a starting point for ligand optimization,' supporting the practical utility claims.

results.result: Background context: IDPs are recognized drug targets; NMR CSP is the best experimental method for identifying drug-interacting residues but can produce small signals within spectral resolution; aromatic residues frequently interact with drugs via π-π interactions with aromatic-rich drug molecules; MD simulations provide atomic details but suffer from force field inaccuracies and sampling issues; drug-interacting residues overlap with residues showing elevated R2 due to local interactions or residual structures, which motivated development of DIRseq from SeqDYN.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this background context without challenge. The editor and reviewers acknowledge the challenge of identifying drug-interacting residues in IDPs and the importance of aromatic interactions. One reviewer explicitly notes 'the discovery is that the IDPs interact with drugs mostly using aromatic residues that are easy to understand, as most drugs contain aromatic rings.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on p27-SJ403 validation (C41-C45). Both evaluations find the DIRseq predictions for p27 binding motifs are well-supported by CSP data with strong correlation (r=0.82). Reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the validation set across 10 IDPs.

Perfect agreement on p21-SJ403 validation (C46-C49, C51). Both evaluations support DIRseq's ability to distinguish strong and weak binding sites with mechanistic explanation. Reviewers accept this as part of the validation demonstrating aromatic interactions.

Perfect agreement on p53-EGCG validation (C52-C56). Both evaluations find DIRseq predictions are supported by CSP and MD simulation data with good correlation (r=0.67). Reviewers accept this as independent validation on a different IDP-drug system.

Perfect agreement on α-synuclein validation (C57-C64). Both evaluations accept the moderate correlation and interpretation of method limitations. Reviewers acknowledge validation across multiple IDPs and note the method's compound-independent nature as both strength and limitation.

Perfect agreement on parameter optimization (C71, C73, C77-C80). Both evaluations support the systematic comparison showing aromatic-only models are insufficient and final parameters are justified. Reviewers accept the optimization while noting 'ad hoc modifications' without challenging results.

Perfect agreement on aromatic anchoring mechanism (C82-C86). Both evaluations strongly support the role of aromatic interactions in drug binding. Reviewers explicitly emphasize 'solid support through examples underscoring the role of aromatic interactions' as a key finding.

Perfect agreement on DIRseq utility with ambiguous CSP data (C87-C98). Both evaluations support the integration of DIRseq predictions with NMR and MD simulation data to resolve ambiguous cases. Reviewers accept this as demonstrating complementary value of multiple approaches.

Perfect agreement on uncertainty (C99-C104). Both evaluations rate this case as UNCERTAIN due to very weak CSP signals and limited experimental validation. Reviewers implicitly acknowledge 'varying depths' of validation and 'coarse' predictions in some cases.

Perfect agreement on integration with mutational data (C105-C111). Both evaluations support DIRseq predictions validated by mutational analysis. Reviewers accept this as part of validation set demonstrating orthogonal experimental support.

Perfect agreement on short IDP case (C112-C118). Both evaluations support the methodological adjustment for short sequences and partial overlap between DIRseq and CSP. Reviewers accept this as part of the 10 IDP validation set.

Strong agreement on integration with qualitative NMR data (C119-C123). Both evaluations support DIRseq predictions validated by chemical shift movements and peak broadening. OpenEval includes C124 while peer review explicitly lists it; both accept multiple lines of evidence approach.

Perfect agreement on complex multi-site case (C125-C133). Both evaluations support the reanalysis of CSP data with stringent thresholds and DIRseq predictions for multiple binding sites. Reviewers accept this as demonstrating complementary value of methods.

Perfect agreement on main findings and novelty (C134-C138). Both evaluations strongly support the novelty, accuracy, and mechanistic insights. Reviewers emphasize this is 'the first sequence-based prediction method' with 'solid support' and highlight aromatic interaction findings.

Perfect agreement on promiscuity and specificity patterns (C139-C149). Both evaluations accept the documented examples of cross-binding and site-specific binding. Reviewers acknowledge these patterns while noting the compound-independent nature affects specificity predictions.

Strong agreement on practical applications (C151-C160). Both evaluations support the proposed applications for fragment selection and complementary use with other methods. OpenEval separates virtual screening claims (C161-C164) while peer review groups all applications together, but both support practical utility.

Partial overlap on virtual screening applications (C161-C164). OpenEval rates these claims as UNCERTAIN due to lack of experimental validation. Peer review groups these with other applications (C151-C160) and supports practical utility generally, though acknowledges speculative nature of some applications.

Strong agreement on methodological development (C15-C17, C25, C29, C32, C34-C35). Both evaluations support the modifications from SeqDYN to DIRseq. OpenEval provides more detailed assessment of parameter choices while peer review notes method 'builds on authors' previous work' without concerns.

Strong agreement on background and motivation (C1-C12). Both evaluations accept the scientific context establishing need for DIRseq. OpenEval separates background (C1-C12) from conceptual foundation (C13-C16) while peer review groups all context together.

Strong agreement on conceptual foundation (C13-C16). Both evaluations support the R2 overlap observation and mechanistic basis for adapting SeqDYN. Peer review groups these claims with broader background (C1-C12) while OpenEval separates them as distinct conceptual foundation.

OpenEval evaluates computational docking methods (C165-C166) as SUPPORTED standard techniques. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not specifically comment on these methodological details for generating illustrative poses.
